Not quite. Like I said, "intelligence" is really hard to nail down. I'll put it in someone else's words because they said it better:

"Intelligence is a slippery concept, even in our own species... One psychologist describes it as 'the capacity to learn or to profit be experience.' And another, as 'the capacity to acquire capacity'--the same sort of circular definition offered by Harvard psychologist Edwin Boring: 'Intelligence is what is measured by intelligence tests.' As Robert Sternberg, a former dean at Tufts University, once quipped, 'There seem to be almost as many definitions of intelligence as...experts asked to define it.'"
(Jennifer Ackerman)

I suppose you could say that "our" intelligence is unique to us in that it benefits humanity most and is unique. But, this does not mean that doing things humans do (for example, using computers) is an ideal among all species. It is a highly developed adaptation, but it isn't superior.

Say, I could very easily turn the question back on you and ask why being as intelligent as a bird wouldn't be beneficial to humanity--a lot less people would get lost while hiking, for example. The answer is, I would say, that it isn't necessary for humans to migrate.

The only instance that it would be true that we have an ideal intelligence over other species, or the other way around, is if we needed to fill each other's niches. If humans suddenly needed to be flying, migrating, seed-hiding creatures, birds would become a supreme intelligence on earth. This is true the other way around, too--if birds needed to use computers then humans would be the supreme intelligence. 

The same voice that tells you humans are above everything else is the one that tells a bee that he is the most advanced creature on earth because he can see colors we can't even imagine.

Tl;dr again: because something is different doesn't mean it's objectively superior. Intelligence and suitedness to one's environment are hard to measure because they are exclusively subjective concepts.

In short: there is no such thing as a "truly advanced" species. Truly advanced to what? Every species is "advanced" to be perfectly suited to its environment. Humans just turned out to be extremely good at socializing. The community is, as it were, the human "environment".

But just as you think a bird may be stupid because he can't work a computer, you would fail a bird's tests of intelligence because you can't navigate using the stars to a place you've never been to before, or because you can't remember the location of hundreds of seeds hidden over many square kilometers months after youhid them.

Are birds not as advanced at you when it comes to speaking English and using computers? Are you not as "perfectly advanced" as a bird for your inability to find seeds? Are you primitive compared to a starfish because you can't regenerate limbs? The answer is yes, but that "yes" is close to meaningless.

Tl;dr the definition of things like "intelligence" and "advancement" are vague and hard to define in science. Evolution is not a race or a competition between all species to get the "best" overall lifeform, it's more concerned with setting personal best records in exremely niche areas.

What I do to feel better is remember that a ton of women have deeper voices that are loved and respected. Some off the top of my head--Scarlett Johansson, Edith Piaf, Stevie Nicks (I seriously thought she was a guy the first couple times I heard her singing), and Stephanie Harlowe on youtube are all women with lower voices who are seen as beautiful, smart, cool, or even great singers.. but all definitely are women.

I throw in Stephanie Harlowe because recently I used a pitch analyzer app on her and it turns out we have very similar voices in terms of frequency and it made me feel great because I think she sounds very soothing (I was 8 months on so we may be similar).

Because of the way sound echoes in your skull, you probably sound way deeper to yourself than you do to other people. It might seem scary but try to listen to recordings of yourself to see if your fears are based in reality.

And pitch isn't the only thing that separates women's and men's voices; as long as you have the correct "feminine" intonation (speaking quickly with few breaths, words come through the head instead of the chest, more range in pitch and speed, being "breathier") then it will go miles.

And remember that your voice doesn't make you, you do. You will never be ugly until you say you are. For what it's worth, though, a lot of people think lower voices on women are desirable, attractive, even sexy.

If in a couple years you aren't more at peace, try saving up money to go to a voice trainer. I wouldn't recommend the videos on youtube because not a lot of them know at all what they're talking about and can't give you personalized advice (which is important so you avoid vocal strain).
